title: I built a full aquarium tower defense game with AI art + AI-assisted code. Here’s the workflow
author: ALSAKHRA
selftext:
I’ve been building **Fish Kingdom**, a tower defense game where your aquarium fish (and plecos with miniguns) defend a Guardian Tower against waves of enemies. It’s live on Android, and here’s how AI fits into the pipeline.

**Art: Google Gemini.** Every creature is a Gemini-generated sprite strip: 64 fish, 75 enemies, 72 bosses, 34 pets/plecos and 126 weapons. What made it work:

* Generate on a flat magenta background, then chroma-key it out, which gives clean transparency
* Animation strips (swim, idle, eat, attack), sliced into frames
* An automated QA pass, because AI art has failure modes: caption text baked into sprites, wrong facing direction, duplicate images, white-background patches. I caught and fixed each of these with scripts.
* Weapons are measured automatically to find where the fist grips them, so 126 guns all sit correctly in the pleco’s hand

**Code: Claude Code** as a pair programmer. The engine is hand-rolled vanilla JS (Pixi.js for rendering only), with fish AI, waves, economy and a Supabase backend. The biggest lesson was to keep the AI honest with tests: every gameplay number lives in one balance file, and a test suite pins it.

**Trailer:** cut automatically from real gameplay, rendered headlessly, plus an ElevenLabs voiceover.

🎮 Google Play: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.fishkingdom.game](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.fishkingdom.game)

Happy to go deeper on any part: the sprite pipeline, the QA scripts, or what AI got wrong. What’s been your biggest AI art consistency problem?
